decision.detail: Rita slides the duplicate reel off its spindle and into the clean paper sleeve. She caps the grease pencil, writes ALMA'S DAUGHTER / FAMILY COPY in block letters along the sleeve's top edge, and tucks the sleeve into her bag. The original stays in its can on the console, under her hand, where it was before Phil opened his mouth. She does not look at him while she does it. When the sleeve is closed she sets the pencil down on the console lip and closes her bag's strap once over her shoulder. One line, flat, not raised: 'You can carry it. I'm not handing it over.' She means the sleeve. The can stays. She zips the bag a second time, slower, and turns back to the monitor feed. The Rivoli house-lights song is not mentioned. The application is not mentioned. The ring is not mentioned again. She pulls the next frame up on the preview monitor and starts counting seconds to the fade-out, which is what she was doing before Phil stood in the doorway with his two-taps and his reaching hands.
decision.intention: Alma's daughter gets the interview. The master stays with Rita. Phil carries the sleeve if he wants to be useful. Nothing else is owed.
decision.words: You can carry it. I'm not handing it over.

decision.detail: Rita's hand closes over the original reel where it sits on the console lip, still in its cardboard core, and she slides it two inches toward herself, under the edge of the audio panel where the grease pencil and the clean sleeve are already stacked. The reel does not cross the table. The envelope with the sealed copy sits in front of Phil. She does not touch the envelope. She does not touch the grease pencil. Her thumb rests flat on the flange of the original, the way you'd hold a book on a nightstand so nobody 'helps' you put it back on the shelf. She looks at him for a beat, then looks at the reel, then back at him. No nod. No smile. She pulls the console drawer open two fingers and closes it again, the small metal click the only other sound in the booth.
